Imagine a self-contained, hypothetical world with only the following conditions, and without any unmentioned factors or causal relationships: Wibl has a direct effect on vubr and zuph. Zuph has a direct effect on uvzi. Vubr has a direct effect on uvzi. Method 1: We look at how zuph correlates with uvzi case by case according to vubr. Method 2: We look directly at how zuph correlates with uvzi in general. To understand how zuph affects uvzi, is it more correct to use the Method 1 than Method 2?

    *   $Wibl \rightarrow Zuph$
    *   $Wibl \rightarrow Vubr$
    *   $Zuph \rightarrow Uvzi$
    *   $Vubr \rightarrow Uvzi$

    Here, $Wibl$ is a common cause of both $Zuph$ and $Vubr$. Consequently, $Zuph$ and $Vubr$ are correlated due to their shared cause ($Wibl$). Since both $Zuph$ and $Vubr$ independently affect the outcome $Uvzi$, the total correlation between $Zuph$ and $Uvzi$ (Method 2) is a mixture of the direct causal effect of $Zuph$ and the spurious correlation induced by $Wibl$ (which correlates $Zuph$ with $Vubr$, which in turn affects $Uvzi$).

2.  **Evaluating Method 2 (Unconditional Correlation)**:
    Method 2 calculates the marginal correlation between $Zuph$ and $Uvzi$. Because $Zuph$ and $Vubr$ are correlated (via $Wibl$), and $Vubr$ causes $Uvzi$, the observed correlation between $Zuph$ and $Uvzi$ will be biased. It will overestimate (or underestimate, depending on the signs of the effects) the true causal effect of $Zuph$ on $Uvzi$ because it conflates the direct path ($Zuph \rightarrow Uvzi$) with the indirect path through the confounder ($Zuph \leftarrow Wibl \rightarrow Vubr \rightarrow Uvzi$).
